reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: An abnormal communication between the perilymph-filled inner ear and the air-filled middle ear, most often at the round or oval window, allowing perilymph to leak
Typically presents with episodic vertigo or unsteadiness, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, aural fullness, and tinnitus

Pressure- or sound-provoked vertigo characteristically worsens with straining, coughing, sneezing, nose-blowing or Valsalva (Hennebert sign and Tullio phenomenon), as pressure changes are transmitted to the inner ear
A positive fistula test - nystagmus or vertigo provoked by pressurising the external canal (tragal pressure or pneumatic otoscopy) - supports the diagnosis
Often follows barotrauma from diving or flying, heavy lifting, head injury, or ear surgery such as stapedectomy, though it may occur spontaneously
A Hennebert sign (pressure-induced eye movement) and Tullio phenomenon (loud-sound-induced vertigo) may be present
Initial management is conservative with bed rest, head elevation, and avoidance of straining; persistent or severe cases undergo surgical exploration and sealing of the leak with a tissue graft
The diagnosis is largely clinical and can be hard to confirm, so a high index of suspicion after a precipitating event is important
reference.pathophysiology: The bony and membranous boundaries separating the perilymphatic space of the inner ear from the middle-ear cleft are normally intact. When this barrier is breached, usually at the round window membrane or the oval window and stapes footplate, perilymph escapes into the middle ear. Sudden changes in middle-ear or intracranial pressure - from barotrauma, straining, or trauma - are then abnormally transmitted to the cochlear and vestibular sensory organs, producing episodic vertigo, disequilibrium, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss. This pressure sensitivity explains why symptoms are provoked by Valsalva, loud sound (Tullio), and external-canal pressure (Hennebert). Continued leakage and the resulting disturbance of inner-ear fluid dynamics can lead to progressive cochleovestibular dysfunction if the defect fails to heal.
additionalInvestigations: Pure-tone audiometry to characterise and monitor sensorineural hearing loss
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to assess the otic capsule and windows
Vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials to help exclude superior canal dehiscence
MRI to exclude a retrocochlear or central lesion
Electrocochleography where available to assess inner-ear function
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or profound sensorineural hearing loss
Features of meningitis, suggesting a communication with the subarachnoid space
Persistent disabling vertigo unresponsive to conservative measures
New cochleovestibular symptoms following recent stapes or other ear surgery
reference.prognosis: Many spontaneous or barotrauma-related fistulae settle with conservative measures, and surgical sealing is effective at relieving vertigo; hearing recovery is less predictable, and established sensorineural loss may be permanent.
pitfalls: Attributing all post-traumatic or post-barotrauma dizziness to a fistula without excluding other vestibular disorders
Confusing it with superior semicircular canal dehiscence, which produces similar pressure- and sound-induced symptoms
Delaying exploration in a patient with progressive hearing loss after ear surgery
Relying on a negative fistula test to exclude the diagnosis, which remains largely clinical

management: Trial conservative management first with bed rest, head elevation and avoidance of straining, heavy lifting, nose-blowing and pressure changes, as many fistulae heal spontaneously
Use stool softeners and vestibular sedatives or antiemetics for symptomatic relief of vertigo and to reduce Valsalva-provoked episodes
Undertake surgical exploration (tympanotomy) with grafting to seal the round or oval window for persistent, disabling or progressive symptoms
Advise avoidance of diving, flying and other barotrauma-inducing activities until the fistula has healed
Monitor hearing with serial pure-tone audiometry, recognising that vertigo often settles but established sensorineural loss may be permanent
Refer to otology and provide vestibular rehabilitation for residual imbalance
